sn46.39:1.1: These trees are all “strangling figs”. They are proverbial in folklore for showing the threat of even the slightest evil ([ja370](), [ja412]()). | E.J.H. Corner describes them in delicious detail in his *Wayside Trees of Malaya* (1940), vol. 1, pp. 664–5 (cited by Bodhi in his note on this discourse).
sn46.39:1.3: _Kacchaka_ here is described as a parasitic strangler, which agrees with [pli-tv-bu-vb-pc11:2.1.6](), where it is said to propagate from the trunk. It is sometimes identified with *Toona ciliata*, the “red cedar”, but that cannot be correct, as it is not a strangler. I translate as “Moreton bay fig” in homage to these magnificent trees that flourish throughout eastern Australia. | _Kapitthana_ is Sanskrit _kapītana_, which Sanskrit sources identify with a bewildering variety of trees. One such, the *Ficus virens* or “white fig”, fits the description here.
